Virtual environments let each Python project keep its own isolated set of packages and even its own Python version, so that differing or conflicting dependencies (e.g., one app needing version 1.0 of a library and another needing version 2.0 or 3.0) do not interfere with each other.
This isolation prevents version clashes and makes it safe to upgrade or change packages for one application without affecting others.

A namespace in Python is a mapping that associates names with objects (typically implemented as a dictionary) and it exists independently for each scope such as built‑ins, a module’s globals, or a function’s locals.

Because each module has its own separate namespace, the names defined inside one module do not interfere with names in another; therefore two different modules can each define a function with the same name without any conflict.

In scikit‑learn, hyper‑parameters are the settings of an estimator that are supplied when the estimator is created (via its constructor) and are not learned from the training data during the fit step.
They control aspects of the model such as regularisation strength, kernel type, number of trees, etc.

(e.g., C , kernel , gamma for an SVC or alpha for a Lasso) and can be tuned by searching over a parameter space, but they are distinct from the internal model parameters that the estimator estimates from the data during fitting.
For imbalanced data this matters because a non‑stratified split can produce a fold that has few or even no examples of the minority class, leading to undefined classification metrics (e.g.
ROC‑AUC) or errors when fitting/predicting.

By preserving the class frequencies, StratifiedKFold ensures each fold includes minority‑class samples, giving more stable and meaningful cross‑validation results (though it can also reduce the observed variability across folds).
To estimate performance with 5‑fold cross‑validation you split the training data into five equal‑sized folds.

Train the model on the other four folds (the “k‑1” folds).
Evaluate the trained model on the held‑out fold and record a performance metric (e.g., accuracy).

After repeating this for all five folds you obtain five metric values, and you summarise the result by taking their average (often reported together with the standard deviation) as the estimated general‑validation performance .

By default a published container port is bound to all host network interfaces (i.e., 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and :: for IPv6) .
A virtual machine runs a full operating system with its own kernel, hardware drivers, and all supporting programs, which adds considerable overhead.

In contrast, a container is just an isolated process that includes only the files it needs and shares the host’s kernel with other containers, making it far lighter and allowing many containers to run on the same infrastructure.
A container registry is the centralized service that stores and manages container images, while a repository is a specific collection of related images inside that registry.
In other words, the registry holds many repositories, and each repository groups one or more versions of a particular image.

Build the image – Run docker build pointing at the directory that contains the Dockerfile (the final “.” supplies the build context) .

Tag (name) the image – Include the -t option with a name that includes your registry namespace (e.g., <YOUR DOCKER USERNAME /my‑image ) when you run the build command, which both builds and tags the image in one step .

Publish (push) the image – Use docker push <YOUR DOCKER USERNAME /my‑image to upload the tagged image.
Use a volume when you need data that the container creates or changes to survive beyond the container’s lifetime—e.g., databases, logs, or any generated content.
Data stored in a volume is not removed when the container is deleted; the volume lives independently, so the files remain and can be attached to another container later.

The alternative documentation is available at /redoc , which is rendered by ReDoc .
When you add the middlewares in that order (first MiddlewareA , then MiddlewareB ), the later‑added middleware becomes the outermost layer.
Request path: MiddlewareB runs first, then MiddlewareA , and finally the route handler.
Response path: after the route handler returns, MiddlewareA runs, then MiddlewareB .
This ordering is described in the FastAPI documentation .

In FastAPI, “dependency injection” is the mechanism by which a path‑operation function can declare the things it needs (“dependencies”), and FastAPI will automatically call the corresponding functions, obtain their results, and pass (inject) those results into the path‑operation’s parameters .

Declaring a separate output model (e.g., UserOut ) as the response model lets FastAPI filter out fields that should not be exposed—such as the password—while the path‑operation function can still return the full object that includes the password.
FastAPI uses the response model to validate, document and convert/filter the response data, so only the fields defined in the output model are sent to the client.
This also avoids type‑checking conflicts, because the function’s return type can remain the internal model (which contains the password) while the response is shaped by the declared output model.
Raise an HTTPException with a 404 status code (and an optional detail message).
FastAPI will convert this into a 404 response with a JSON body like {"detail":"Item not found"} .
To test a FastAPI app with TestClient you:
Add the HTTPX dependency (TestClient is built on it).
Import TestClient – you can import it from fastapi.testclient (a convenience wrapper) or directly from starlette.testclient .
Create a client instance by passing your FastAPI app object to TestClient .
Write test functions whose names start with test (the pytest convention).
Inside those functions call the client (e.g., client.get("/") , client.post(...) ) just like you would with HTTPX/Requests, and assert on the response (status code, JSON body, etc.).
Optionally, keep your tests in a separate file (e.g., test main.py ) alongside the app module and use relative imports to bring in the app object.
FastAPI looks at the signature of the path‑operation function:
If the parameter name also appears in the URL template, FastAPI treats it as a path parameter.
If the parameter is a simple (singular) type such as int , float , str , bool , etc., it is taken from the query string .
If the parameter is declared as a Pydantic model , FastAPI reads the whole request body into that model.

For query parameters, FastAPI decides whether they are required by the presence of a default value: a parameter without a default is required, while giving it a default (e.g., = None ) makes it optional.
The str None annotation does not affect this; the default value does.
You schedule a background job by calling the add task() method on a BackgroundTasks instance, passing the function to run and any arguments it needs.
If you declare a BackgroundTasks parameter both in a dependency (or sub‑dependency) and directly in the path‑operation function, FastAPI re‑uses the same BackgroundTasks object.
All tasks added at any level are merged together, and the combined set of background tasks is executed after the response is sent.

Amazon S3 provides strong read‑after‑write consistency for both PUT and DELETE operations on objects—any read (GET or LIST) that follows a successful PUT or DELETE response will see the newly written data or the deletion, respectively.
The standard Init phase can run for up to 10 seconds .

If the three required tasks (starting extensions, bootstrapping the runtime, and running static function code) are not finished within that window, Lambda retries the Init phase when the function is first invoked, using the function’s configured timeout as the new limit .

For functions that use provisioned concurrency, SnapStart, or Lambda Managed Instances , the 10‑second limit does not apply; initialization may run for as long as 15 minutes (capped at 130 seconds or the function’s configured timeout, whichever is higher) .
When an Init‑phase timeout or crash occurs, Lambda records the failure in an INIT REPORT log entry .
An IAM user is a permanent identity that belongs to a specific person or application and has its own long‑term credentials.

An IAM role is also an identity with permissions, but it is not tied to a particular person ; instead it is assumed by users, services, or other principals and provides temporary credentials for the duration of the session.
This makes roles useful for granting permissions without creating a separate user for each actor.
A cold start happens when Lambda receives a request and must create a new execution environment.
During this initialization phase the service downloads the function code, sets up the runtime, runs any static‑initialization code outside the handler, and then invokes the handler.
This extra work adds latency (typically 100 ms to 1 s) and is billed as part of the init time .
A warm start occurs when a subsequent request arrives while the previously created execution environment is still retained.
Lambda skips the download and setup steps and reuses the already‑initialized environment, so the invocation finishes more quickly .
To create a Lambda execution role with the AWS CLI you use the aws iam create‑role command and supply a trust policy that lets the Lambda service assume the role.
Create the role – Provide a role name and a trust‑policy document (either inline or from a file).
Attach permissions – After the role is created, attach the needed managed policies (e.g., the basic execution role):
These steps create a Lambda execution role that the Lambda service can assume and give it the initial permissions you attach.
Enable provisioned concurrency or SnapStart .
Provisioned concurrency initializes execution environments in advance and keeps them ready, so invocations start from a warm environment with predictable, low‑latency latency.

SnapStart creates a snapshot of the initialized environment when you publish a version, allowing Lambda to restore that snapshot instantly for each invocation, also giving consistently low start times.

That trio—bucket + key + optional version—uniquely identifies each object, and the same components are used to form the object’s URL (e.g., https://{bucket}.s3.{region}.amazonaws.com/{key} ) for addressing it.
An S3 bucket policy is an IAM resource‑based policy —a JSON‑formatted policy that is attached directly to a bucket rather than to a user, group, or role .

To let another AWS account access the bucket, you create (or update) a bucket policy that specifies that account’s AWS account ID and grants the desired S3 actions (e.g., PutObject) on the bucket or its objects, then attach that policy to the bucket .
